text:
# Prescriptive lessons — ted-greene × single-note-soloing-vol-1

## any

Greene's foundational architecture applies uniformly across every chord quality: the major scale is the single reference system from which all chord formulas and scale relationships are derived numerically, the eighth note is jazz's default rhythmic unit, and every run must be practiced in both swing and straight feel. Technique, register awareness, and fingerboard visualization are cross-cutting requirements with no chord-quality exceptions.

1. Derive every chord and scale relationship from the major scale using numeric scale-degree notation. The major scale is the universal reference: "G is the 4th of D" means G is the 4th tone of the D major scale; this numeric logic governs all intervals, chord formulas, and scale modifications throughout the book. (ch.1 p.8)
2. Understand that a chord "takes" a scale when that scale sounds good played over it — this is the governing pairing concept for all chord-scale decisions. (ch.1 p.10)
3. Organize all single-note soloing around three questions: what notes sound good over the chord, where those notes are on the fingerboard, and how to play them interestingly. (ch.1 p.6)
4. Treat the eighth note as the primary rhythmic unit for jazz single-note lines at medium and fast tempos. Great players create fluid lines by running long streams of 8th notes through multiple measures. (ch.3 p.39)
5. Practice every 8th-note run in both swing feel and straight feel. Both feels are required for contemporary music; neither is optional. (ch.3 p.39)
6. Produce swing feel by interpreting written straight 8ths as triplets with the middle note tied or missing — the ear hears two notes interpreted as "funny" 8th notes. (ch.3 p.39)
7. Use double-timing — running 16th notes at medium or even fast tempos — as an advanced texture option over any chord quality. (ch.3 p.40)
8. Achieve cleanliness before increasing tempo. Gradually push tempos upward, but only after playing cleanly at the current speed. (ch.3 p.40)
9. Understand the trill as decoration of a held note, not substitution of one note for another. The note being trilled is still present — it is enhanced, not replaced. (ch.3 p.41)
10. Place trills predominantly on the strong part of the beat. Experiment, but strong-beat placement is the default. (ch.3 p.41)
11. Confine hammer-on target notes to tones found within the currently active scale. Hammer-ons to non-scale tones are outside scope at this level. (ch.3 p.41)
12. Do not use hammer-ons as standalone jazz melodic devices at this stage. Their role here is as a component of the trill; isolated hammer-ons (except the grace note, covered in Volume II) are not standard jazz guitar practice. (ch.3 p.41)
13. Interpret "b7" as "the 7th tone lowered by a half-step," not as a guarantee that the resulting note will be spelled with a flat. (ch.3 p.41)
14. Try every run pattern an octave higher within the same fingerboard position. This is a standing practice rule throughout Chapter 7. (ch.7 p.120)
15. Finger each set of scale runs in at least one alternate fingerboard position to expand positional fluency. (ch.6 p.109)
16. Fret with the pad of the finger, not the tip. (ch.6 p.111)
17. Identify and target melody notes within scale runs at every chord-quality level. Melodic note selection within scalar material is prescribed across major, dominant, minor 7th, and altered dominant chapters. (ch.2–5 passim)

---

## maj

The major triad (formula 1, 3, 5) is the foundational building block from which all major chord types extend. It establishes the natural third and fifth that define the major sound and carry into maj7, maj9, and beyond.

1. Know the major triad formula as 1, 3, 5 derived from the major scale. This is the base from which maj7 and all major extensions are built. (ch.1 p.9)

---

## maj7

Greene treats maj7 chords as members of "major Group 1," pairing them with either the major scale or the Lydian scale — a choice of personal preference rather than harmonic necessity. The Lydian option's #4 is its sole distinguishing color and is characterized as the "hippest" of the two. Fingerboard visualization and position-based combining of these two scales are Greene's primary prescriptions for realizing maj7 soloing on the instrument.

1. Know the maj7 chord formula as 1, 3, 5, 7 — all derived from the major scale. These are the chord tones of any major 7th chord in its root position. (ch.1 p.9)
2. Assign maj7 chords to the "major Group 1" harmonic family. This family membership determines which scales are available and how runs are selected. (ch.1 p.9)
3. Over maj7 (Group 1 major) chords, use either the major scale or the Lydian scale. The choice is almost always personal preference — both sound good in most cases. (ch.1 p.10)
4. Understand the Lydian scale as a major scale with a #4 in place of the natural 4th. This single raised fourth is the only difference between the two available scale options. (ch.1 p.10)
5. Use the major scale's upper-partial extension system to understand maj7 chord extensions: adding the 9th produces a ninth chord (1, 3, 5, 7, 9); adding the 11th produces an eleventh (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11); adding the 13th produces a thirteenth (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13). The 11th shares a letter name with the 4th; the 13th shares a letter name with the 6th. (ch.1 p.10)
6. Stay within a 5–6 fret fingerboard area when soloing over maj7 chords. Know enough positions of both the major and Lydian scales to navigate a whole song without shifting out of that area. (ch.4 p.60)
7. Actively visualize the notes on the fingerboard while playing — do not rely on rote pattern recall. Fingerboard visualization is "one of the best things you can do for yourself" when soloing over major Group 1 chords. (ch.4 p.67)
8. Apply major and Lydian scale runs in 3/4 time for jazz waltz feel when variety is desired. (ch.4 p.71)
9. Use chord arpeggios (chord tones 1, 3, 5, 7 played successively) as foundational soloing material alongside scalar runs over maj7 chords. (ch.2 pp.11–40)

---

## min

The minor triad formula (1, b3, 5) establishes the lowered-third characteristic that carries into all minor chord types, including min7 and its scale pairings.

1. Know the minor triad formula as 1, b3, 5 derived from the major scale. The b3 is the defining interval of all minor chord types. (ch.1 p.9)

---

## min7

Greene pairs min7 exclusively with the Minor 7th scale (major scale with b3 and b7), explicitly prohibiting the relative-major shortcut. The ii-V-I progression is the recommended learning context, and position-based combining of the min7 scale with the major and dominant 7th scales is the fingerboard realization method.

1. Know the min7 chord formula as 1, b3, 5, b7 derived from the major scale. For a C minor 7th, this yields C, Eb, G, Bb. (ch.1 p.9)
2. Pair min7 chords with the Minor 7th scale — a major scale with lowered 3rd (b3) and lowered 7th (b7). This is the prescribed scale; no other is introduced for vanilla min7 at this stage. (ch.4 p.66)
3. **Do not** think of the Minor 7th scale as a major scale starting a whole step below the chord root. Even though the notes are identical, internalizing the scale from a foreign root will impede later development. Root-based thinking is mandatory. (ch.4 p.69)
4. Learn and practice min7 runs within the ii-V-I progression context. The ii-V-I is one of the most common progressions in jazz and the most practical context for internalizing m7 runs at this stage. (ch.4 p.67)
5. Combine min7 scale runs with major and dominant 7th scales within a single 5–6 fret fingerboard position so that the full ii-V-I can be navigated without shifting. The "Combining Scales in One Position" technique is explicitly named for this purpose. (ch.4 p.60)
6. Use minor 7th type arpeggios alongside scalar runs as core soloing material over min7 chords, studied within the ii-V-I context. (ch.5 pp.86–105)

---

## dim

The diminished triad formula (1, b3, b5) defines the fully contracted sound of the diminished chord type. No further scale-pairing or soloing rules for diminished chords are introduced in this volume.

1. Know the diminished triad formula as 1, b3, b5 derived from the major scale. (ch.1 p.9)

---

## aug

The augmented triad formula (1, 3, #5) defines the sound of augmented chords and reappears as the upper structure of augmented 7th chords in the altered dominant context.

1. Know the augmented triad formula as 1, 3, #5 derived from the major scale. (ch.1 p.9)

---

## dom7

Greene introduces the Dominant 7th scale (major scale with b7) as the exclusive pairing for dom7 chords and prohibits the common shortcut of treating it as a major scale starting a 4th higher. He further subdivides dominants into Group 1 (without the 11th, requiring runs with the 3rd) and Group 2 (with the 11th, requiring runs with the 11th), and treats register as a primary variable in how extensions like b7 and 9 are perceived.

1. Know the dom7 chord formula as 1, 3, 5, b7, derived from the major scale with a lowered 7th tone. (ch.3 p.41)
2. Pair dom7 chords with the Dominant 7th scale — a major scale with a lowered 7th tone. Any chord built from only these tones can take this scale; chords containing tones outside this set fall outside the pairing. (ch.3 p.41)
3. Apply the scale-chord compatibility rule strictly: only chords whose tones are drawn exclusively from the Dominant 7th scale's chord-tone set may take that scale. (ch.3 p.41)
4. **Do not** treat the Dominant 7th scale as a major scale starting a 4th higher. Internalizing it from a foreign root will make things harder later. Build all Dominant 7th scale knowledge from the chord's own root. (ch.3 p.43)
5. For Group 1 dominant chords (chords without the 11th), select runs that contain the 3rd. Runs containing both the 3rd and the 11th, or neither, are usable over both groups. Watch ending and lingering tones. (ch.4 p.59)
6. For Group 2 dominant chords (chords that include the 11th), select runs that contain the 11th. (ch.4 p.59)
7. Treat register as a primary variable in how b7 and 9 are perceived over dominant chords. In a "higher" register (even if still relatively low on the instrument), b7 and 9 function as spicy mid-range colors rather than heavy bass tones. (ch.4 p.58)
8. Combine major and Dominant 7th scales within a single 5–6 fret fingerboard position to allow seamless soloing across I–V chord changes without shifting. (ch.4 p.60)
9. Apply Dominant 7th scale runs in 3/4 time for jazz waltz feel across both Group 1 and Group 2 dominant contexts. (ch.4 p.71)
10. Use dom7 type arpeggios alongside scalar runs as core soloing material. Arpeggio tones may also be played on the 5th and 4th strings, not only the highest strings, extending reach within the position. (ch.4 pp.61–85; ch.6 p.107)

---

## dom7#11

Greene classifies dom7#11 chords as Group 3 dominants, pairs them with the Overtone Dominant (= Lydian Dominant) scale, and draws a hard categorical boundary: the #11 is not an alteration in the chromatic sense but a reflection of the overtone series. The 9, #11, and 13 form an upper-structure major triad a whole step above the root — the named device of polytonality.

1. Pair dom7#11 (Group 3 dominant) chords with the Overtone Dominant scale — a Dominant 7th scale with a #4 (#11) in place of the regular 4th. This scale is also called the Lydian Dominant scale. The #11 is its single distinguishing feature. (ch.4 p.82; ch.5 p.83)
2. **Do not** classify the Overtone Dominant / dom7#11 as an altered dominant chord. The #11 reflects the overtone series, not chromatic alteration; it is not a b5 even if it enharmonically coincides with one. (ch.5 p.94)
3. Over a dom7#11 chord, identify the polytonal upper-structure major triad formed by the 9, #11, and 13 of the Lydian Dominant scale. These three "hippest" tones form a major triad rooted a whole step above the chord root. Exploiting this relationship is the device of polytonality (to be covered fully in Volume II). (ch.5 p.83)
4. Before attempting Overtone Dominant / Group 3 runs, be able to visualize the Group 3 chord forms in that position. If run visualization is difficult, return to the chord forms first — chord form visualization is the prerequisite to scalar fluency. (ch.5 p.99)
5. Use Overtone Dominant arpeggios alongside scalar runs as core soloing material over Group 3 chords. Arpeggio tones may be played on the 5th and 4th strings as well as the highest strings. (ch.6 pp.106–120)

---

## dom7alt

Greene defines altered dominants by the presence of at least one of four altered tones (b9, #9, b5, #5/b13) and groups all such chords into Group 4. Three Altered Dominant scale types are prescribed, and they are taught simultaneously in the same fingerboard position — the "package deal" — so color differences between nearly identical scales are absorbed comparatively.

1. Define an altered dominant chord as any dominant 7th type chord containing one or more of: b9, #9, b5, or #5 (b13). All such chords belong to Group 4 Dominant Chords. (ch.5 p.94)
2. Learn all three Altered Dominant scale types in the same fingerboard position simultaneously (the "package deal"). Their near-identity means the brain can absorb all three together, and juxtaposition makes their subtle color differences more evident, accelerating both learning and ear development. (ch.5 p.96)
3. Before attempting Group 4 altered dominant runs, return to Group 4 chord forms in the position if run visualization is difficult. Chord form visualization is the prerequisite to scalar fluency for all altered dominant work. (ch.5 p.99)
4. Do not construct or expect Type 3 altered dominant material for fingerboard Area 4A. This absence is an instrument-specific structural constraint, not an oversight. (ch.7 p.118)
5. Extend altered dominant arpeggio patterns into the upper register using the supplementary higher-register arpeggio section, in addition to the standard fingering-area exercises. (ch.7 p.133)
6. Use Altered Dominant arpeggios alongside scalar runs as core soloing material over Group 4 chords, across Areas 4A, 5, and 5A. (ch.7 pp.121–137)

---

## dom7b9

Dom7b9 chords are a subset of Group 4 altered dominant chords. All Group 4 prescriptions apply.

1. Classify any dominant 7th chord containing b9 as a Group 4 altered dominant chord. The b9 is one of the four defining altered tones (b9, #9, b5, #5/b13), and its presence alone is sufficient for Group 4 membership. Apply all Group 4 altered dominant scale and practice rules. (ch.5 p.94)

---

## dom7#9

Dom7#9 chords are a subset of Group 4 altered dominant chords, with an additional substitution allowance: the #9 may replace or supplement the natural 9 in altered dominant exercises.

1. Classify any dominant 7th chord containing #9 as a Group 4 altered dominant chord. The #9 is one of the four defining altered tones. Apply all Group 4 rules. (ch.5 p.94)
2. In altered dominant passages, the #9 may be used instead of or in addition to the natural 9. This substitution applies across altered dominant exercises. (ch.7 p.131)

---

## dom7b5

Dom7b5 chords are a subset of Group 4 altered dominant chords. All Group 4 prescriptions apply.

1. Classify any dominant 7th chord containing b5 as a Group 4 altered dominant chord. The b5 is one of the four defining altered tones (b9, #9, b5, #5/b13). Its presence alone qualifies the chord for Group 4 membership and all associated scale pairings. (ch.5 p.94)

---

## aug7

The augmented 7th chord (dom7 with #5) is a Group 4 altered dominant chord and also carries a standing substitution allowance within Type 3 altered dominant exercises.

1. Classify aug7 (dominant 7th with #5/b13) as a Group 4 altered dominant chord. The #5 (b13) is one of the four defining altered tones. Apply all Group 4 altered dominant scale and practice rules. (ch.5 p.94)
2. In Type 3 altered dominant exercises, A7+ (augmented 7th) may be substituted for A7#9+. This substitution allowance is a standing rule applying across all subsequent Type 3 pages. (ch.6 p.105)
